soil-hist-106.title: Edmund Ruffin and the marl that revived worn-out fields
soil-hist-106.text: More than a century of tobacco monoculture had worn the land out when a young planter began spreading marl on it. Edmund Ruffin (1794–1865) was an American planter, politician and scientist, and he started these experiments in his twenties. Marl, a calcareous earth, was his main tool. He recommended crop rotation and amendments for exhausted soils. He studied bogs and swamps to learn how to correct soil acidity, and he tried lime to raise the pH of peat soils. His book An Essay on Calcareous Manures explained how marl had cut acidity and raised corn and wheat yields. Few farmers took his advice in his own time. He has since been called the father of soil science in the United States. Yet he is best known as an early advocate of secession of the Southern slave states, and he farmed his plantations with enslaved labor.

soil-hist-105.title: Edgar Buckingham names the pull of soil on water
soil-hist-105.text: Edgar Buckingham spent only four years as a soil physicist, yet textbooks still cite him. The American physicist (1867–1940) worked at the USDA Bureau of Soils from 1902 to 1906. He began with aeration: how carbon dioxide leaves soil and oxygen replaces it. Gas diffusion, he found, barely depended on structure, compactness or water content. He gave the diffusion coefficient as an empirical function of air content. Soil gas exchange, he concluded, runs by diffusion and largely ignores outside barometric pressure. His water work appeared in 1907 as Bulletin 38, Studies on the movement of soil moisture. Soils can strongly inhibit evaporation, he showed, especially where capillary flow through the top layers is cut off. He named the capillary potential arising from soil–water interactions, now called matric or water potential. He was the first to tie hydraulic conductivity to that potential, applying a formula equivalent to Darcy's law to unsaturated flow.

soil-hist-108.title: Joseph Henry Gilbert, the chemist behind Rothamsted's long trials
soil-hist-108.text: Some field experiments Joseph Henry Gilbert started in 1843 are still running. Gilbert (1817–1901) was an English chemist and a former doctoral student of Justus von Liebig at Giessen. In 1843 he became director of the chemical laboratory at Rothamsted, the experiment station of John Bennet Lawes. He stayed from that June until his death, and he conducted most of the meticulous studies published under both names. That same year the two men began their long-term field experiments. The results contradicted Gilbert's old teacher. Cereal crops, they found, take up nitrogen from the soil, while Liebig had held that it came only from the air. Their work made Rothamsted a leading center of agricultural research.

soil-hist-109.title: Konstantin Gedroits and the soil that holds on
soil-hist-109.text: Konstantin Gedroits (1872–1932) wanted to know how soil holds what it holds. The Russian soil scientist, of Lithuanian origin, founded colloidal soil chemistry in Russia. He introduced the concept of the soil absorbing complex. He also split soil absorption capacity into three types: mechanical, physico-chemical and biological. He then classified soils by composition. Soils unsaturated with cations stood apart from those saturated with calcium, and from those saturated with sodium ions. The same chemistry explained how saline soils evolve. It also laid the theoretical basis for liming and for adding gypsum to soil. Gedroits led the chemistry laboratory of the Dokuchaev Soil Institute in 1915–17 and headed the institute in 1929–30. He received the Lenin Prize in 1927, and from 1927 to 1930 he was president of the {{ref:soil-hist-047}}.

soil-hist-104.title: Charles Darwin and the worms beneath the loam
soil-hist-104.text: Shown ground where cinders had vanished under loam, Charles Darwin named a culprit: earthworms. The English naturalist, geologist and biologist (1809–1882) is best known for evolutionary biology. His five-year voyage on HMS Beagle, from 1831 to 1836, made him an eminent geologist. On 1 November 1837 he presented his theory of the earthworm's role in soil formation to the Geological Society. He came back to worms at the very end. His final book, The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Actions of Worms (1881), counts among his works of great importance.

soil-hist-110.title: Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure finds plant carbon in the air
soil-hist-110.text: Where does a plant get its carbon? Most of Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure's immediate predecessors said from soil humus. The Swiss chemist and plant physiologist (1767–1845) showed that it comes from carbon dioxide in the air, which made him a major pioneer in the study of photosynthesis. He studied plant gas exchange and how different soils affected growth, gathering the work in Recherches chimiques sur la Végétation (1804). Unlike some before him, he based his conclusions on extensive quantitative data. He also showed that plants need mineral nutrients taken up from the soil. That disproved the idea that plant minerals arose by transmutation inside the plant. His findings were largely neglected for decades. Then Liebig revived them and used them to critique humus theories, and Boussingault's field research confirmed the importance of soil mineral nutrients.

soil-hist-103.title: Albrecht Thaer puts farming into a system
soil-hist-103.text: Albrecht Thaer trained as a physician and loved flower gardening before he turned to agriculture. The German agronomist (1752–1828) became known across Europe for applying science to farming practice. He is described as the first agricultural scientist to arrange the existing facts and theory of agriculture into a proper system. In 1802 he founded the first German agricultural training institute at Celle, where he experimented with crop rotation to raise yields. In 1804 came the first German agricultural academy, at Möglin, renamed the Royal Prussian Academy of Agriculture in 1819. The academy analyzed many soils and classified them by dominant component, such as sand, lime or red and blue clay, each marked with a colored label. This classification came into common use on large German estates. His four-volume Grundsätze der rationellen Landwirthschaft (1809–1812) covered the theory of soil, plowing, manuring and irrigation. It appeared in English in 1844 as The Principles of Agriculture. Its humus theory of plant nutrition was still accepted in the period 1800–1860.

soil-hist-107.title: Francis D. Hole, the pedologist who gave Wisconsin a state soil
soil-hist-107.text: Wisconsin has an official state soil, Antigo silt loam, because Francis D. Hole campaigned for it. The legislature named it in 1983. Hole (1913–2002) was an American pedologist, educator and musician. He created the periodical Soil Survey Horizons in 1960 and co-created the Soils of Wisconsin Map of 1968. With Stanley Buol and Ralph McCracken he wrote Soil Genesis and Classification, first published in 1973 and used worldwide. His Soils of Wisconsin (1976) followed Hans Jenny's factors of soil formation and divided the state into regions A to J.

soil-hist-111.title: Thomas Lyttleton Lyon and the Cornell field plots
soil-hist-111.text: Principles of Soil Management went through 10 editions. Its author, Thomas Lyttleton Lyon (1869–1938), was an American soil scientist who wrote on the nitrogen cycle. From 1912 he headed the department of soil technology at the Cornell University College of Agriculture. At Cornell's Caldwell Field he ran many field studies, including lysimeter and plot experiments. In 1913 he and James A. Bizzell won the Howard N. Potts Medal for a paper on how certain non-leguminous plants relate to soil nitrate content. He had been publishing soil science textbooks since 1907.

soil-hist-112.title: Milton Whitney, a chief whose views met resistance
soil-hist-112.text: Milton Whitney was the first chief of the US Division of Agricultural Soil, the forerunner of the federal soil survey. He held firm views on soil chemistry and fertility, and the evidence did not always agree. Franklin Hiram King found that nutrient concentration in the soil solution correlated with crop yield, which undermined those views. Whitney's ideas also shaped what the Bureau released. George Nelson Coffey's map never became an official Bureau map, because it did not fit Whitney's prevailing soil classification concepts.

soil-hist-113.title: Nikolai Sibirtsev, Dokuchaev's partner in a new science
soil-hist-113.text: Nikolai Sibirtsev (1860–1900) led the Russian school of soil science together with Vasily Dokuchaev. From 1870 that school, under the two men, developed a new concept of soil. Sibirtsev taught soil science as a professor. When he fell ill, Konstantin Glinka took over his teaching. He is also counted among the Russian geographers who made great contributions to physical geography.

soil-hist-136.title: Geoderma, an international journal of soil science
soil-hist-136.text: Geoderma is an international soil science journal. In 1967 Roy Simonson became its editor-in-chief, and he published numerous articles in its pages.

soil-hist-137.title: The Viking landers ask Martian soil if anything lives there
soil-hist-137.text: In 1976 two landers scooped up Martian soil to test it for life, and scientists still argue over the answer. The Viking landers carried four biological experiments to the surface of Mars to look for microbes. Viking 1 worked near the equator and Viking 2 farther north, each loading soil into sealed chambers with a robotic arm. A gas chromatograph–mass spectrometer, sensitive to a few parts per billion, found no significant organic molecules. Martian soil held less carbon than lifeless Apollo lunar soil. Fed nutrients and water under helium, soil in the gas exchange experiment made oxygen disappear on contact and kept giving off carbon dioxide. The pyrolytic release experiment exposed soil to carbon-14-labeled CO and CO2, then baked it at 650 °C to detect carbon fixed as biomass. Any positive result was to be checked on a heat-sterilized duplicate: persisting activity meant chemistry, a lost response meant biology. The general view blames oxidative reactions, since constant ultraviolet light has given the soil a thin layer of very strong oxidant. Yet perchlorate, found by Phoenix in 2008, destroys organics on heating and yields chloromethane and dichloromethane, the very compounds Viking detected. A 2018 reanalysis suggested organics may in fact have been detected, matching Curiosity rover data. Whether the results reflect soil chemistry alone or could include biology remains disputed.

soil-hist-139.title: Bringing pieces of Mars back to Earth
soil-hist-139.text: Of over 79,000 known meteorites, 356 had been identified as Martian by August 2023. A proposed sample-return mission would add a second source: rock and dust collected on Mars and brought to Earth. Returned samples would allow far more extensive analysis than onboard sensors, focused on whether Mars once hosted life. Future instruments could reanalyze them. The Perseverance rover, landed in Jezero crater in February 2021, is caching rock, regolith and atmosphere samples for return. Some have raised the risk of Martian organisms contaminating Earth, but the scientific consensus is that large-scale effects are unlikely.

soil-hist-140.title: Growing plants in space, and on the Moon
soil-hist-140.text: The first plant grown on the Moon survived 2 days. It was cotton, sprouted in January 2019 in a sealed biosphere on the Chang'e 4 lander. Most space plants grow instead in pressurized, weightless space gardens in low Earth orbit. Weightlessness is the first challenge, because gravity matters for root development, soil integration and watering. For long-term growth, nutrient supply to roots, biogeochemical cycles and microbial life in soil-based substrates are particularly complex. University of Florida tests showed Arabidopsis thaliana can germinate and grow in lunar soil, but slowly and with signs of stress.

soil-hist-138.title: The labeled release test and its disputed signal
soil-hist-138.text: The labeled release experiment dosed Martian soil with a dilute nutrient solution tagged with radioactive carbon-14, then watched the air above for labeled gas. On both landers the first injection gave a steady stream of radioactive gas, from a sunlit surface sample and from one beneath a rock. Samples heated 3 hours at 160 °C released no gas, and at 50 °C much less. But second and third doses released no more gas Living terrestrial soil would have. Superoxides formed by ultraviolet light, or hypochlorite from irradiated perchlorate, may explain the result chemically. Its designer, Gilbert Levin, and Straat maintain the results indicate life. Most astrobiologists judge them inconclusive or negative, the work of oxidizing soil chemistry.
